title: The Gap Between Me and the Machine
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky opens his year-long theme of digital wellness by turning the lens on himself, tracing how three years of working with generative AI in teaching, writing, and research have changed his relationship to the tool. He argues first that duration of use is a poor proxy for impact, and that any honest assessment has to weigh immersion, multitasking, and the effects of AI on memory, thinking, and agency. He then narrates his arc: early suspicion prompted by student plagiarism, a decision in 2023 to lean in, the exhausting quality-control burden of early tools, and the later agentic explosion that made building easy but introduced new tradeoffs. The turning point comes as he grows skeptical of AI feedback and of the sameness of AI prose, and he describes an unsettling distance from his own AI-assisted work, borrowing Brian McHale's idea of an ontological flicker. He closes by redirecting his work away from AI literacy as such and toward building students' background knowledge, work habits, domain skills, and agency, since most schools lack the capacity for the deep redesign the technology would demand.
points: Potkalitsky argues that screen-time duration says little about impact, and that the real questions concern immersion, multitasking, and AI's effect on memory, thinking, and agency.
The promised six hours a week of AI time savings were, in his experience, consumed by managing bots and policing output quality over long work cycles.
He grew wary of AI feedback on his own work after seeing how perspectival it is and how canned AI prose became, and began deliberately distancing himself from the tools.
Trust built with his own students around AI could not be handed to other teachers, which pushed him to anchor AI work in each teacher's content area instead of generic AI literacy.
His new priority is building students' knowledge, organization, domain skills, and agency, since most schools cannot undertake the redesign AI would require.
quotes: This is a long way of saying that duration alone is not a great measurement of impact. Alongside, we have to think about the distractive or immersive qualities of those engagements, the level of multimodality and multi-tasking required to sustain said engagement, and the affective, psychological, and social consequences of short-term and prolonged use.

The promise at that time was AI was going to save you 6 hours a week. But for me, that 6 hours was quickly filled up with the management of bots and the quality control of output across extended workcycles. AI gave me a work assistant, but one that didn't listen very well and required constant hand-holding.

In essence, I had built a deep trust with my students through my honesty and vulnerability about these new tools (challenges and opportunities). This trust empowered transformation. But you cannot develop that trust for other teachers.

Perhaps the reasoning was growing stronger, but the articulation of that reasoning was becoming increasingly canned and overladen with quirky AI-isms. It all started sounding the same. As a result, I continued to put greater distance between myself and AI as I developed projects I wanted to share with others.
A tool that I once thought augmented my intellectual process and research, I now understood as something of a detriment.

But I have come to recognize that most schools do not have the infrastructure or the willingness to engage in the deep instructional redesign this technology demands. So our continued work must now focus on the building up of our students: their background knowledge, their organizational skills and work habits, their domain-specific skills and competencies, their sense of agency, empathy, and individuality, etc.
